result.summary: The 1,000-1,412 range is the collection, merge, and emit layer, and it is where the index stops being an index. Measured against the working tree: 771 raw ontology nodes collapse to 701 by `node["name"].lower()` alone (:1320) — 51 name keys collide across 51 DIFFERENT texts (zero same-text duplicates), 70 records are absorbed, 14,066 characters of definition text are discarded, and in 32 of 51 merges the surviving definition comes from one book while the surviving greek/type/centralityTier come from another, producing composite records that cannot be attributed to any single source. 119 tension records are reachable on disk; 64 are emitted; 55 are dropped in silence by the `node_a`/`node_b` guard at :1128-1129 plus the bare `if edge:` at :1110 (Burke GM 16, Calleja 12, Gross 15, Wendt 12). The compiler emits exactly ZERO warn() lines on the current corpus — I measured it — while doing all of that, and the docstring at :14-15 promises "Malformed rows/entries are skipped with warnings to stderr." There is no argparse, no sys.exit, no assert, no error counter, no --strict (grep returns nothing), no CI job references the compiler, and the one test that touches the artifact (tests/data-integrity/test_reasoning_edges.py:74-78, "no duplicate ontology names") is tautological: it asserts the postcondition of the `by_name` dict at :1318-1320 and cannot fail. Determinism is dead twice over: `builtAt` at :1375 is stamped unconditionally, and `canonicalTerms` is a `set` (:1283) sorted on `(-len(t), t.lower())` (:1304), which leaves 101 tie groups / 202 terms ordered by set-iteration; I proved the flip empirically by re-running the exact sort under PYTHONHASHSEED 1/2/3/random and getting four different SHA-256 digests of the emitted order. Additional live wrong-output: `_infer_target_text` tests `"physics" in lower` at :1067 BEFORE `"metaphysics" in lower` at :1069, so the Metaphysics arm is unreachable dead code and `_infer_target_text("Metaphysics Lambda")` returns "Physics" — hook-physics-12 and hook-physics-13 are emitted pointing at their own source work; and 0 of 72 hooks carry a targetText that joins to any node's `text` label or any TEXT_DIRS/ARISTOTLE_WORK_MAP value. 54/64 tension edges have a nodeA and 57/64 a nodeB that match no ontology node name; 52 join to nothing on both ends. `collect_cross_pipeline_hooks` hardcodes the Aristotle directory at :1239 and globs only under it at :1244, so all 72 hooks are Aristotle by construction. `collect_ontology_nodes` iterates the hardcoded TEXT_DIRS allowlist (:1185), so 8 of the 27 real directories under corpus/index are invisible, three of them holding a `_synthesis/cluster-ontology.md`; I parsed RDR2 Secondary's (35 concept bullets) with the header parser and got 0 nodes, with no warning — registering it would change nothing. Net throughput: 30.9 MB of .md/.json/.csv under corpus/index becomes a 664 KB artifact (2.15%); the 91 KB of Aristotle hook markdown becomes 10,132 characters of retained prose. `_normalize_tension_edge`'s return dict (:1165-1174) silently drops 13 distinct input keys across the surviving 64 records, including `locus_a`/`locus_b` (the page anchors), `provenance`, `works`, `interp_level`, `chapters`, and `node_c` (one three-node tension flattened to two). No emitted record of any type carries an id-with-provenance, a source filename, a line offset, or a page: `ontologyNodes` has exactly ten fields and none of them is addressable.

findings.claim: canonicalTerms is emitted from a Python set with a sort key that ties for every case-variant pair, so 202 of 1,722 term positions are ordered by PYTHONHASHSEED-dependent set iteration.
findings.evidence: :1283 `    terms: set[str] = set()`; :1303-1304 `    # Sort by length descending (greedy matching), then alphabetically\n    return sorted(terms, key=lambda t: (-len(t), t.lower()))`. `t.lower()` makes 'Logos'/'logos' compare equal on both key components; sorted() is stable, so the tie is resolved by set iteration order.

Reproducing the exact set->sorted path under PYTHONHASHSEED=1/2/3/random gave four different SHA-256 digests of the emitted order: 803cfafa…, ddf51ab5…, 1fa67772…, 02af165a… . Feeding the same terms in reversed insertion order flips exactly 202 positions.

Worse, the sort's stated purpose ('greedy matching') has no consumer: smart-retrieval-layer.ts:268-270 uses `canonicalTerms.filter(t => t.length >= 4 && queryLower.includes(t.toLowerCase()))`, which is order- and case-insensitive.

findings.claim: For the Uexküll alternate format the compiler writes the SAME value into dependencyRelation and conflictRelation, manufacturing a dependency claim the source never made, and discards the tension's own label.

findings.claim: `units` is passed through with a type check for str only; any other JSON type lands in the artifact unvalidated.

findings.claim: build_canonical_terms tests the length of the RAW translation but adds the STRIPPED value, so it can emit 1-character and even empty canonical terms — the exact case the `len(cleaned) > 1` guard four lines above exists to prevent.

findings.consequence: An empty canonical term poisons every substring consumer: smart-retrieval-layer.ts:268-270 filters on `t.length >= 4` and survives, but corpus-index-provider.ts:175-191 builds keyword sets from node terms without a length floor, and any `includes('')` test is universally true. Zero occurrences today; one bolded short Translation cell away from live.
findings.fix_sketch: Strip first, then test. 3 lines.

findings.claim: canonicalTerms mixes true lemmas with whole analytical sentences, and separately drops the short Greek lemmas that matter, because the length policy is set here but the usable range is decided downstream.

Downstream, smart-retrieval-layer.ts:268-269 `const queryTerms = canonicalTerms.filter(t =>\n            t.length >= 4 && queryLower.includes(t.toLowerCase())\n          );`

At the other end, 13 terms are <4 chars and therefore unreachable by the only consumer, including the Greek lemmas 'ὕλη' (matter), 'ἁφή' (touch), 'φῶς' (light), plus 'HMD', 'IVR', 'PIM', 'SSQ'.

findings.claim: Hook bridge and relevance are truncated to their first sentence at emit time, so two thirds of the analytic prose in the hook files never leaves the compiler.

findings.claim: No emitted record of any type carries an identity or a provenance anchor: ontologyNodes has ten fields and not one of them is an id, a source file, a line offset, or a page.

        "greek": greek,
        "transliteration": transliteration,
        "translation": translation,
        "definition": strip_bold(definition),

findings.failure_scenario: Ask 'where does this definition come from?' of any merged node: `text` says 'Aristotle - Complete Works; Aristotle - Metaphysics; Aristotle - Physics' and nothing narrows it further — and corpus-index-provider.ts:121-126 does not render `text` at all, so the model sees the definition with no attribution whatsoever.
findings.consequence: This is the single largest obstacle to the stated goal. Claim- and clause-level records are worthless without stable addressability; adding it requires the parsers to track offsets, which none of them do.
findings.fix_sketch: Thread an offset through each parser (enumerate over splitlines with a running char count), emit {id: sha1(text+name)[:12], sourceFile, startLine, endLine}. ~120 lines across the four parsers — the largest single change, and the one that has to happen first.

findings.claim: The artifact is a single monolithic JSON document, pretty-printed, re-serialized in full on every build, tracked in git, and parsed synchronously twice per Node process.

Node parses it in 3.8 ms for 5.7 MB of heap — a 8.6x in-memory expansion — and does so twice. The current uncommitted diff is 583 insertions / 55 deletions on this one file.

findings.claim: The only automated check on compiled-index.json is tautological: it asserts the postcondition of the dict used to build the array, so it cannot fail no matter how badly the merge corrupts the data.

findings.fix_sketch: Golden-file test: run the compiler into a temp dir over a 3-entry fixture corpus and diff against a checked-in expected artifact; assert counts per text and assert zero silent drops. ~80 lines, and it needs the compiler to accept --out first.

findings.claim: The 'copy' in deduplicate_ontology_nodes is shallow, so an unmerged node's units/aliases lists are shared with the raw input object.

findings.claim: The latin-1 decode fallback can never fail, so a mis-encoded file yields mojibake Greek that flows into names and canonicalTerms with only a single stderr line.

findings.claim: The compiler writes its 664 KB output into the very directory tree it scans, and the ingest pipeline's SKIP_DIRS does not exclude corpus/index.

findings.consequence: Derived data re-enters the corpus as if it were a source, inflating the collection with machine-generated text; at 100x the artifact this becomes the largest single 'document' in the store.
findings.fix_sketch: Write to a build/ directory outside corpus/, or add 'index' to SKIP_DIRS. 1 line either way — but choose deliberately, since the artifact's path is hardcoded in three TS files.

architecture_assessment.current_capability: Concretely, today: the compiler walks a hardcoded 19-entry allowlist (TEXT_DIRS :35-133) over 19 of the 27 real directories in corpus/index, runs four markdown/table parsers plus one JSON normalizer, and emits a single 664,494-byte pretty-printed JSON document with four arrays — 701 ontologyNodes (10 fields each: name/greek/transliteration/translation/definition/type/units/text/aliases/centralityTier, produced at :495-506, :379-390, :663-674, :756-767), 72 crossPipelineHooks (9 fields: id/sourceText/sourceConcept/targetText/targetConcept/title/bridge/relevance/tag, produced at :898-908, :963-973, :1015-1025), 64 tensionEdges (8 fields: id/text/nodeA/nodeB/dependencyRelation/conflictRelation/description/units, produced at :1165-1174), and 1,722 canonicalTerms strings (:1276-1304), assembled at :1374-1380 and written at :1384-1387. That is a concept gazetteer with a thin cross-reference layer, and the measurements say so: 30.9 MB of .md/.json/.csv under corpus/index becomes 664 KB, i.e. 2.15% of the source bytes survive; the 91 KB of Aristotle hook markdown yields 10,132 characters of retained prose; 19,770 CSV edge rows across 192 *-edges.csv files, 34 units/*.md files, 22 manifest.json files, 5 citation-network.md and 5 debate*.md files are never opened by this script at all. What actually reaches a prompt is narrower still: corpus-index-provider.ts:101-103 caps injection at 12 nodes / 3 hooks / 5 tensions, truncates each definition to 200 chars (:124) and each unit list to 5 (:125), and never renders the `text` field — so the model receives concept names, a Greek lemma, two sentences of gloss, and no provenance. The prior audit's summary ('concept names and little else') is, if anything, generous.
architecture_assessment.ceiling: Four hard walls, in the order they are hit. (1) Correctness, already breached: the merge key `node["name"].lower()` (:1320) collides for 51 of 701 names at today's volume — 7.3% — and every collision is cross-book. Claim-level records make this catastrophic, because claim text is not a stable key at all; a name-keyed dict cannot express 'the same claim asserted by two authors' versus 'two different claims that share a phrase'. (2) Container: measured 712 bytes per node and 706 per tension edge. 224 ingested documents at a conservative 200 claims each is ~45,000 claim records -> ~32 MB pretty-printed; clause-level at 10 clauses per claim is ~450,000 records -> ~320 MB. Node reads this through readFileSync+JSON.parse twice per process (jsonl-loaders.ts:210-211 and smart-retrieval-layer.ts:800), measured at 3.8 ms and 5.7 MB heap for 664 KB — an 8.6x heap expansion, so 320 MB of JSON is ~2.8 GB of heap per parse and ~1.8 s of blocked event loop, twice. V8's max string length puts a hard ceiling near 512 MB on readFileSync('utf-8') regardless of RAM. The practical wall is ~30-50 MB, i.e. roughly 50x, and that assumes no other memory pressure. (3) Git: the artifact is tracked and rewritten in full every build (current diff: 583 insertions / 55 deletions), with `builtAt` (:1375) and 202 hash-ordered term positions (:1283/:1304) guaranteeing a diff even for a no-op run. A 32 MB tracked file that churns on every build makes the repository unusable for review. (4) Build time is the one thing that does NOT break: the parsers are linear over file bytes and would still run in seconds at 100x.
architecture_assessment.claim_level_readiness: Five changes, in dependency order, and the first is the expensive one. (a) IDENTITY AND ANCHORS. Nothing emitted today is addressable — no id, no sourceFile, no line, no page, on any of the three record types. Every parser iterates `for line in text.splitlines()` (:244, :335, :577, :701) and tracks no offset, so anchors cannot be retrofitted at the emit site; each parser must thread a running offset. ~120 lines across four parsers, and no claim-level work is meaningful before it lands: a claim record without a locus is not evidence. Note the corpus already knows this — the tension files carry locus_a/locus_b and evidence_pages_pdf, and the compiler throws them away at :1165-1174. (b) LOSSLESS PASSTHROUGH. The three return dicts are fixed projections; 13 distinct input keys are dropped from tension edges alone. Claim-level records will arrive with fields nobody anticipated (modality, hedging, quantifier scope, negation, page span). The emit layer must carry unknown keys rather than silently discarding them. ~20 lines but a schema decision. (c) A REAL MERGE POLICY, or none. Name-lowercase merging must be replaced by (text, name) identity plus explicit sameAs links, with per-field provenance. At claim level, dedup is a similarity problem, not a dict lookup — which means the merge belongs in a database with an index, not in a Python dict comprehension. (d) VALIDATION WITH TEETH. No warn fires today while 55 records vanish; there is no exit code, no counter, no --strict, no CI job, and the single test (test_reasoning_edges.py:74-78) asserts the dict's own postcondition and cannot fail. At 45,000 records, silent drops are undetectable by inspection — this stops being a hygiene issue and becomes the only thing standing between the user and a quietly half-empty index. (e) A DIFFERENT CONTAINER. Per-entry JSONL shards or SQLite with indices on (text, name), (claimId), (nodeAId, nodeBId); the consumer stops parsing 300 MB to inject 12 records and starts querying. jsonl-loaders.ts already implements the mtime-cache pattern that would front it.
architecture_assessment.harden_or_replace: Replace the emit layer; keep the parsers as adapters; and above all keep the corpus, which is the real asset. The evidence for replacing rather than hardening lines 1181-1412 specifically: the collection layer is a hardcoded allowlist that has already silently lost 8 of 27 directories (:1185), the hook collector is one directory literal (:1239), the tension collector is one filename literal (:1267), the merge is a name-lowercase dict that fabricates composite records (:1320-1348), the emit is a fixed projection that drops 13 known-good fields (:1165-1174), and the whole thing has no exit code (:1361-1412). Every one of those is a structural choice, not a bug — hardening them one at a time means rewriting the same 250 lines five times while the artifact stays unaddressable. Against replacement stands the parser layer, and it should be defended: :195-767 handles four genuinely different markdown dialects that real analysts produced over a year, it works (771 nodes with no exceptions raised), and rewriting it would be pure risk. Even the one parser that fails — RDR2 Secondary's `- **Name** — gloss — units · Tier` bullets, which yield 0 nodes — fails by omission, not by corruption. So: lift :195-1025 out as a per-format adapter package (they are already nearly pure functions of (text, label)), give each adapter offset tracking and an `extra` passthrough, and rewrite :1181-1412 as a schema-first loader that discovers entries from _synthesis/manifest.json (22 already exist on disk), validates every record against a declared schema, assigns stable ids with file+line anchors, writes JSONL shards or SQLite, refuses to publish on zero-node parses or unexplained count drops, and exits non-zero. Two immediate, near-free wins to take regardless of the larger decision: delete `builtAt` at :1375 or replace it with a content hash, and make the merge key (name, text) so that the 51 cross-book collisions stop fabricating composites — those two changes alone make the artifact reviewable and its provenance honest, which is the precondition for trusting anything built on top of it.

result.summary: The out-of-band couplings in this repo are worse than the string-grep ones, because nothing reports them. Three structural facts dominate. (1) Both GitHub workflows are unrunnable-by-construction: god-learn/knowledge.jsonl, god-learn/index.json, god-reason/index.json and all 292 corpus PDFs are untracked, so a fresh CI checkout cannot satisfy artifact_loader.py:132-136, verify_knowledge.py:30-31, or 22 of the 24 entries in the immutability baseline; separately, the four audit core scripts the workflow invokes directly raise ModuleNotFoundError unless PYTHONPATH=scripts is set, a coupling that exists only as `env: PYTHONPATH: scripts` at god-audit.yml:31 and is documented nowhere else (verified by execution: `env -u PYTHONPATH python3 scripts/audit/core/missing_link_detector.py --help` → "No module named 'explore'"). (2) The immutability gate is currently RED and has been silently red since 2026-01-13 — I reproduced verify_immutability()'s exact comparison and got 17 violations (9 baseline files missing, 8 mutated, including three Aristotle PDFs and all five JSONL/JSON artifacts); manifest.jsonl went from 21 lines in the baseline to 1,182 today. The protected list at :111-122 covers PDFs and knowledge JSONL but NOT corpus/index and NOT compiled-index.json, so the index the user actually cares about has zero integrity protection while 1.5 GB of PDFs get SHA-256'd on every run. There is also no mechanism for a legitimate change: the only remedy is --baseline (:202-231), which rewrites all 24 entries wholesale. And `--verify --json` returns 0 even on violations (:405-406 prints and falls through; the `return 1` at :434 lives only in the else-branch). (3) The blast radius of moving corpus/index is small (11 code files) but the blast radius of RENAMING one entry directory is large and mostly invisible, because the coupling is a hardcoded whitelist: TEXT_DIRS at compile-corpus-index.py:35 lists 19 directories, 8 real entry directories exist on disk that are not in it (Red Dead Redemption 2 Playthrough + Secondary, three Aristotelian Secondary clusters, Game-Behavior Analysis Method, Veri(dis)similitude, Dissertation — 686 files, 452 markdown), and collect_ontology_nodes warns only in the forward direction (:1186-1188), never that a directory exists and was skipped. I confirmed empirically from compiled-index.json that none of those 8 contribute a single node. normalize-edges.py:35-42 repeats the same pattern at a smaller scale: 5 of the 20 global-edges.csv files on disk, plus one entry whose path is simply wrong. Also found: a complete config layer (scripts/common/config.py, paths.corpus_root + GOD_LEARN_PATHS_CORPUS_ROOT) with exactly zero consumers; provenance_tracer.py:363-367 resolving PDFs by basename and then reporting verified=True on a hash of possibly the wrong file; 6 corpus-root path joins (2 more than the 4 claimed) plus 7 cwd-relative index loads; 16 hardcoded /home/dalton paths in code (zero in src/).

findings.claim: The baseline stamps a naive local-time timestamp and is a tracked file, so every re-baseline produces a git diff whose most visible change is a clock reading.

architecture_assessment.current_capability: Concretely, today, this code can: (a) parse ~290 hand-authored markdown files under 19 whitelisted directories in corpus/index/ into a single 664 KB compiled-index.json holding 701 ontology nodes, 1,722 canonical terms, 72 cross-pipeline hooks and 64 tension edges; (b) load that file into Node with an mtime-keyed cache (jsonl-loaders.ts:199-217) so a recompile is picked up without a restart; (c) use it at runtime for three narrow purposes — exempting canonical terms from stopword filtering (smart-retrieval-layer.ts:794-810), licensing concept pairs for reasoning (reason_over_knowledge.py:192-214), and deriving cross-author bridges and tensions (cross-author-utils.ts). What it carries into runtime is concept NAMES plus a small amount of per-node metadata (name, greek, transliteration, translation, definition, type, units, text, aliases, centralityTier — the actual key set I read off node 0). The 'units' field is an array of unit IDs — pointers to markdown, not content. There is no claim record, no clause record, no span, no offset, no page anchor, and no quotation anywhere in the compiled artifact. Separately there is a real ingestion path (scripts/ingest/*, ChromaDB, 1,182 manifest lines) that carries chunk text with page ranges — but as the census shows, nothing joins the two: the compiled index has no chunk_id and the chunks have no ontology node.
architecture_assessment.ceiling: The ceiling is not throughput, it is registration. Three hard numbers. (1) TEXT_DIRS is a 19-entry hand-maintained literal at compile-corpus-index.py:35 and there are already 8 unregistered entry directories on disk containing 686 files and 452 markdown documents contributing exactly 0 nodes. The whitelist broke at 27 entries — it is broken NOW, silently, and the breakage grows monotonically with authoring. (2) normalize-edges.py:35-42 covers 5 of 17 real global-edges.csv files; 12 entries' edges are dropped on every --all run behind a single [SKIP] on stderr. (3) The compiled index is a single 664 KB JSON blob read whole, JSON.parse'd whole, and cached whole at jsonl-loaders.ts:210-213. At 100x — call it 70,000 nodes and 172,000 terms — that is roughly a 65 MB parse on every mtime change, in-process, synchronous (readFileSync at :210). smart-retrieval-layer.ts:800 parses it a SECOND time independently. And the only integrity check that exists, immutability_checker.py:134-142, hashes 1.5 GB per verify with a 4 KB read loop and no mtime pre-filter, running every 5 seconds in watch mode (:386) — at 100x that is ~150 GB per pass. The volume ceiling and the registration ceiling arrive at the same place: the system stops being able to tell you what it is missing.
architecture_assessment.claim_level_readiness: Carrying claim- and clause-level records at 100x needs four things this code does not have, and none of them are a tweak. FIRST, stable identity. There is no ID scheme for a claim or a clause anywhere. The compiled index keys nodes by name (the merge in deduplicate_ontology_nodes keys on name.lower() with no text component), and the only durable IDs in the repo are ingestion-side: doc_id = sha256(f'{path_rel}:{sha256_file}')[:16] with chunk ids {doc_id}:{idx:05d}. A claim record needs an ID derived from (doc_id, page, char-span, text-hash) so that it survives re-ingest and can be cited. Building that is real work, but it is the ONE piece that makes everything else possible. SECOND, a store that is not a single JSON file. 70,000 nodes each with claims and clauses is a queryable store — SQLite with FTS5 plus the existing Chroma vectors is the obvious shape, and it kills the whole-file parse, the double parse at smart-retrieval-layer.ts:800, the two uninvalidated module-globals (_hooksDerivationDone at cross-author-utils.ts:56, protectedTerms at smart-retrieval-layer.ts:795), and the mtime cache in one move, because a database invalidates per row. THIRD, registration by discovery rather than by literal. Every whitelist in the compiler must invert: enumerate corpus/index/*, read a per-entry config that lives WITH the entry, and warn on anything unregistered. This also fixes the entry-rename blast radius described below. FOURTH, integrity that scales and that actually runs. Whole-file SHA-256 over 1.5 GB of PDFs is the wrong primitive; append-only ledgers need prefix-immutability checks and derived artifacts need count/shape assertions (node count, term count, per-entry contribution) rather than byte hashes. The honest sequencing: identity scheme → store → discovery-based registration → integrity. Steps 1 and 2 are weeks; steps 3 and 4 are days once 1 and 2 exist.
architecture_assessment.harden_or_replace: Harden the ingestion and retrieval spine; REPLACE the compiled-index layer and the audit/immutability layer. The evidence splits cleanly. Worth keeping: the ingestion path has genuine engineering in it — content-addressed doc_ids, a 1,182-line manifest, page ranges on chunks, a working Chroma store, and a reranker the user has already evaluated. That is a foundation and it should be extended, not rewritten. Also worth keeping: corpus/index/ itself. The 335 tracked markdown files under 27 entry directories are the actual intellectual asset and they are in a sane, human-authorable, git-friendly format. Nothing about the data needs replacing. What must be replaced is the thin, brittle layer between them. compile-corpus-index.py is a 1,412-line single-pass markdown scraper whose registration mechanism is a Python dict literal that is already wrong by 8 entries, whose output is a monolithic JSON blob, whose only 'connection' primitive (cross-pipeline hooks) is hardcoded to one author's directory at :1239, and which — per the prior audit and confirmed by the 0/72 sourceAuthor measurement — emits fields so incomplete that a downstream module has to re-derive them at runtime behind a never-reset global. Hardening that means fixing the whitelist, fixing the glob, fixing the merge key, fixing the determinism, and adding warnings — at which point you have rewritten it anyway, and you still have a monolithic JSON blob that cannot hold a clause. The audit/CI layer should be deleted rather than fixed: two workflows, ten entrypoints, and I could not find evidence any of it has ever completed a run — three of five immutability-protected files are untracked, four of six audit scripts need an undocumented PYTHONPATH, the vector_db_1536 trigger is gitignored, qa/baselines and qa/reports do not exist, and the immutability gate has been red since 2026-01-13 with 17 violations nobody has seen. Replace it with three checks that run on every compile and exit non-zero: every corpus/index directory is registered, every global-edges.csv is consumed, and the compiled artifact's node/term counts did not drop. Those three would have caught every finding in this report. On the two blast radii the task asked me to separate: MOVING corpus/index is cheap — 11 code files hold the literal (4 Python, 6 TypeScript, 1 test), of which the load-bearing ones are compile-corpus-index.py:31, jsonl-loaders.ts:200, smart-retrieval-layer.ts:798, merge-reasoning-edges.py:21, reason_over_knowledge.py:199, normalize-edges.py:37-41, test_reasoning_edges.py:18; the remaining ~55 markdown files and 307 in-corpus data files are prose and regenerable data. Call it a day's work. RENAMING a single entry directory is the expensive one and it is expensive precisely because the couplings are not greppable: you must edit the TEXT_DIRS key at compile-corpus-index.py:35+ (and know that the 'label' is a separate field, so downstream 'text' values only survive if you change the key and NOT the label); you must edit normalize-edges.py:37-41 if it is one of the five, and its PATH_HINTS substring table at :44+; if it is Aristotle you must also edit :1239 and ARISTOTLE_WORK_MAP or all 72 hooks vanish; deriveAuthor's ABBREVIATION_MAP in cross-author-utils.ts and its manifest-canonical lookup key off the label; ChromaDB metadata path_rel values are persisted and NOT re-derivable without re-ingest; scripts/ingest/manifest.jsonl carries path_rel and the only delete path (run_ingest_phase2.py:1830, fed by a where={'path_rel': ...} query) returns zero rows once a path changes, so stale chunks are unreachable and unpurgeable; and the immutability baseline stores paths as strings, so a rename reads as a deletion — I can demonstrate that exact failure today, since 9 of the current 17 violations are nothing but filename drift. That is at minimum six code sites, one re-ingest, one manual purge, and one re-baseline, with silent partial failure at every step. Entry names are load-bearing identifiers scattered across three languages and two databases with no indirection layer. Introducing a stable per-entry slug — decoupled from the display name and from the directory name — is the single highest-leverage change available, and it is a prerequisite for the claim-level work, not a separate project.

result.summary: In my range the compiler is not an index builder; it is a lossy concept-name scraper with the error reporting disabled by construction. Measured on the live corpus: 48 of 1,848 files are opened (2.60%); the only structured output per concept is a 10-key flat dict with NO file, line, section, or page provenance (:379-390, :495-506), so nothing it emits can ever be traced back to a clause. warn() (:153-154) is real and writes to stderr, but a full read-only collection over the entire corpus emits ZERO warnings — every one of the 8 warn sites reachable from my range is either guarded by a condition that is false today (:1188/:1193/:1205/:1229 — all files present), wrapped around code that cannot raise (:286-287, :318-319 — verified no IndexError path exists), or gated on non-UTF-8 input that does not exist (:161-163). The docstring's "Malformed rows/entries are skipped with warnings to stderr" (:14-15) is false in both halves: entries ARE skipped, at a minimum of 20 distinct in-range sites, and NONE of those sites warns. Live data loss confirmed today: 6 four-column cross-work claim rows in de-anima-ontology.md (φύσις/τόπος/χρόνος/ῥητορική/τέχνη/πάθος with their loci) are dropped by `len(cells) < 5` at :260; 96.8% of the 9,867-char tail of metaphysics-ontology.md — including the 14 numbered Key Positions with Bekker loci and status — is absorbed into the ὄρεξις node and discarded, because :308 splits the whole file and the last section runs to EOF; 70.2% of all cross-pipeline-hook prose (23,843 of 33,975 chars) is thrown away by first_sentence() at :171-181; parse_units() at :188 splits on whitespace and has put 968 lowercase English word-fragments and 35 bare "|" tokens into the shipped canonicalTerms/units; and the title splitter at :350 has shipped a node literally named "Contradiction (PNC)" (from "Principle of Non-Contradiction"). Three registered directories' worth of the file layout is one missing trailing pipe away from silent corruption: :409 only builds the header map when the data row's cell count exactly equals the header's, so a single ragged row falls through to positional parsing that reads the definition column as units and emits an empty definition — same table, same file, no warning. Output is not reproducible even ignoring builtAt: four separate processes produced four different canonicalTerms digests, because :1304 sorts a set on a key with 101 exact ties. This is a foundation only in the sense that the markdown source files are good; the compiler is an obstacle and should be replaced, not hardened.

findings.claim: The abbreviation guards in first_sentence are mis-assigned to the wrong letters: 'e.g.' is NOT protected (it ends in 'g'), and the `(?<!\bi)` guard protects nothing.
findings.evidence:
:174 `    # Match up to the first period followed by whitespace or end-of-string,`
:175 `    # but skip common abbreviations like "e.g.", "i.e.", "cf."`
:176 `    m = re.search(r'(?<!\be)(?<!\bi)(?<!\bcf)(?<!\bvs)\.\s', text)`
findings.failure_scenario: Verified: first_sentence('See e.g. Aristotle DA II.5. The second sentence follows.') returns 'See e.g.' — truncated after two words. The `(?<!\be)` lookbehind happens to protect 'i.e.' (whose final letter is 'e'), while nothing protects the 'g' of 'e.g.'. `(?<!\bi)` can only fire on a standalone trailing 'i', which never occurs. findings.fix_sketch: Replace the lookbehind stack with an explicit abbreviation set checked against the token preceding the period. ~10 lines.

architecture_assessment.current_capability: Within lines 1-520 the code does exactly one thing: it turns markdown concept tables into a flat list of 10-key dicts {name, greek, transliteration, translation, definition, type, units, text, aliases, centralityTier}. On the live corpus that is 771 raw dicts from 48 files (2.60% of the 1,848 files under corpus/index), deduplicated to 701 and flattened into 1,722 canonicalTerms. It reads exactly four filename patterns (book-level-ontology.md, cluster-ontology.md, Aristotle/*-ontology.md, Aristotle/*-cross-pipeline-hooks.md, plus tension-edges.json) from a hand-maintained 19-entry allowlist at :35-133. It handles three markdown dialects (pipe rows, field/value tables, header/bullet) with per-dialect ad hoc parsers that disagree with each other on tier vocabulary (:372-377 open vs :478 closed), on the meaning of `type` (:385 centrality vs :501 node-type), on the unknown sentinel ("" vs "unknown"), and on parenthetical cleaning (:361 strips, table path does not). It does NOT extract claims, clauses, spans, page/line anchors, or edges between claims — tensionEdges and crossPipelineHooks come from separate hand-written JSON/markdown, not from analysis. It cannot fail: no argparse, no assert, no exit code, and the one diagnostic channel (warn, :153-154) emits nothing on the current corpus.
architecture_assessment.ceiling: The breaking point is not throughput, it is silence, and it has already been crossed. Concrete numbers from this range: 48 of 1,848 files read; 8 of 27 content directories unregistered, 3 of them holding a complete cluster-ontology.md that contributes 0 nodes; 8 of 56 candidate tension paths absent with no warn; 6 de-anima cross-work claim rows dropped at :260; 9,867 chars of metaphysics tail absorbed and 96.8% discarded via :308; 23,843 of 33,975 chars (70.2%) of hook prose discarded by :171-181; 3,099 chars (12.6%) of field text — including all 26 global_candidate flags — dropped at :379-390; 968 shredded prose tokens and 35 bare '|' characters sitting in units arrays from :188; one centralityTier field holding 10,009 chars. Runtime is not the constraint: the whole build is 48 file reads and a few thousand regex operations, well under a second. At 100x volume (~4,800 registered ontology files, ~77,000 nodes) the wall clock is still seconds, but the registry at :35-133 would need ~1,900 hand-written entries, the O(n^2) header substring scan in get() at :421-424 becomes noticeable, and — decisively — the silent-loss rate stays proportional while the operator's ability to spot it goes to zero, because the only feedback is a printed node count at :1391 and there is no baseline to compare it against.
architecture_assessment.claim_level_readiness: Four things are missing and none of them is a patch. (1) Provenance: the node dict at :379-390 and :495-506 has no slot for source_path, line span, section anchor, or a stable id. Every parser signature — parse_table_ontology(text, text_label), _parse_field_value_section(section, text_label) — takes bare text with the file already forgotten by :1201/:1213/:1225, so a (path, lineno) cursor has to be threaded through all five parsers and every call site. Without that you cannot cite a clause, and the user's own citation-rigor rule makes an uncitable index worthless. (2) A record model above concept: claims, clauses, and edges need to be first-class row types with their own schemas. The corpus already CONTAINS them — metaphysics-ontology.md `## 3. Key Positions` is 14 numbered claims each with a Bekker locus and a status, and this code absorbs all 14 into the ὄρεξις node's fields dict as keys '1'..'14' and drops them at :379-390. The data exists; the schema has nowhere to put it. (3) A real parse layer: a claim-level index cannot be built on regex line-scanning that misroutes an entire file on one `| Field | Value |` line (:216), loses a whole table to a missing separator row (:275-279 + :409), and infers importance from the first letter of a cell (:481-486). It needs a markdown AST with tables as structured nodes, so column identity is a parse result rather than a substring guess. (4) Enforcement: schema validation, a warn counter, --strict, a nonzero exit, and a golden-file diff. Because the output ordering is nondeterministic across processes (four runs, four digests), even the diff is impossible until :1304 gets a total sort key. Item (2) alone is a new data model; items (1) and (3) are a rewrite of every function in my range.
architecture_assessment.harden_or_replace: Replace the parsing layer; keep the corpus and the registry idea. Hardening arithmetic from lines 1-520 only: the fix list is ~15 CRITICAL/HIGH items, of which the cheap ones (:1304 total sort, :350 dash class, :188 split class, :228 slice end, :439/:440-441 dead code, :1268 else/warn) total under 30 lines — and none of them moves the system toward claim-level records; they only stop it lying. The expensive ones are structural: provenance threading through five parsers, a markdown AST to replace :244-289 and :335-344, a claim/clause record model, and a validation harness. That is a larger diff than rewriting the ingest as an AST walk over the same markdown with a versioned schema, and the rewrite arrives with the provenance the current design has no slot for. Three pieces of evidence make the case that this is not a fixable design. First, the author already tried to teach it about a table type it silently vetoes: :270 lists 'targeted concept' as a recognised header, and the only such table in the corpus (de-anima-ontology.md:57, 4 columns) never reaches that line because :260 drops it first — a later guard silently disabled an earlier feature and nothing reported it. Second, the same unbounded-section bug exists independently in two parsers (:308 in my range, the :718 break outside it), which is what happens when three dialects get three hand-rolled scanners instead of one grammar. Third, and decisively, the docstring at :14-15 has promised stderr warnings since the file was written and the mechanism emits nothing at all on the live corpus — the design has been failing silently for its entire history with no observability, and every number in this report had to be recovered by re-running the parsers by hand. Verdict: the markdown corpus under corpus/index is an excellent foundation and should not be touched; scripts/compile-corpus-index.py is an obstacle and should be replaced with an AST-based, provenance-carrying, schema-validated, fail-loud compiler. Do the ~30 lines of cheap fixes first, but only to stop the bleeding while the replacement is built.

findings.evidence:
retrieval-stage.ts:226 — `const id = c.metadata.chunk_id || `${c.metadata.source_id}:${c.metadata.page_start}`;`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:972-990 builds metadata with exactly: author, title, year, page_start, page_end, collection, doc_id, chunk_index, path_rel, content_type, has_bboxes, source_method, bboxes — no `chunk_id`, no `source_id`.
scripts/ingest/run_ingest_phase2.py:1737-1753 — `chunk_metadata = { "doc_id": doc_id, "chunk_index": c.chunk_index, "path_abs": ..., "path_rel": ..., "collection": ..., "sha256": ..., "mtime": ..., "page_start": c.page_start, "page_end": c.page_end, ... }` — no chunk_id, no source_id written to Chroma either.
