architecture_assessment.current_capability:
Measured, not estimated. The read path can take a topic string, do case-insensitive substring matching over 701 ontology node names/definitions, 72 hooks and 64 tension records held entirely in memory, and emit at most 12 + 3 + 5 pre-rendered markdown lines into a prompt. For the topic 'The phenomenology of boredom in VR pedagogy and attunement' that is 5,271 characters out of a 656,755-character index — 0.803%. Of the ten fields each ontology node carries, four reach a prompt (name-or-greek, transliteration, definition truncated at 200 chars, first 5 unit IDs); translation, type, text, aliases and centralityTier are never rendered by any code path. Of the eight fields each tension carries, five reach a prompt; dependencyRelation and conflictRelation — the analytic content — are neither searched nor rendered. It is, precisely as the brief suspected, a concept-name carrier. It carries no claims, no clauses, no character offsets, no page locators, no document IDs, and no scores. loadCorpusIndexContext returns three arrays of formatted strings (corpus-index-provider.ts:159); by the time data crosses the module boundary it has already been flattened into prose and every structural handle is gone.

Worse, on this corpus it does not reliably do even that. getActiveBridges — the function behind the 'MANDATORY THEORETICAL SYNTHESIS' block — returns hook-de-anima-07 for essentially any input, including the nonsense words ['zzzzz','qqqqqq'], because 31 of 72 hooks have an empty targetConcept and `t.includes('')` is always true (cross-author-utils.ts:474). That hook has empty targetText, targetConcept, bridge and relevance, so the prompt instructs the model to cite an author named 'Unknown'. The corpus catalog injected into decomposition prompts lists 117 of 578 titles under the header 'only suggest from this list' and mislabels 71 of those 117 as SECONDARY SCHOLARSHIP — including Heidegger's *The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics* and the Greek critical editions of De Anima, Physica and Ars Rhetorica.
architecture_assessment.ceiling: Four separate walls, in the order they are hit. (1) The caps bind NOW, at 1x. maxOntologyNodes 12 / maxHooks 3 / maxTensions 5 (corpus-index-provider.ts:101-103), 1 bridge (:498), 3 tensions (:542) are absolute integers, not proportions. Measured discard on a real topic: 67 nodes scored above zero, 12 emitted, 55 dropped with no count and no log. At 100x volume the emitted context is byte-for-byte the same size while the discard rate goes from ~82% to ~99.8%. The system does not get slower as the corpus grows; it gets proportionally blinder, silently. (2) readFileSync into a single JS string. Node v22.22.0 MAX_STRING_LENGTH is 536,870,888. god-reason/reasoning.jsonl is 21,498,945 bytes today, so the hard throw is at 24.97x — not 100x. At jsonl-loaders.ts:89 that RangeError is UNCAUGHT (process death); the identical read at :210 is inside the bare catch at :215 (silent null, total index blackout). Two different undiagnosable failures from one cause. (3) buildCorpusCatalog is the one component that DOES scale linearly, and that is the problem: 8,439 chars / ~2,110 tokens for 117 titles today, so ~844 KB / ~211,000 tokens at 100x, injected uncapped into every decomposition prompt (llm-decomposition-provider.ts:102-103). Blows any context window at roughly 90x. (4) CPU is the least of it but is real: I timed loadCorpusIndexContext's node scan at 1.94 ms for 701 nodes, extrapolating to ~194 ms per call at 70,100 nodes — synchronous, on the main thread, constructing a fresh RegExp per (term, node) pair. getActiveBridges goes 0.126 ms -> 6.52 ms from 72 to 7,200 hooks, called once per facet. checkSingleTitle goes 0.001 ms -> 0.275 ms from 6 to 6,000 titles per author, called per citation per sub-title, re-running two regex replaces over every title on every call even though the normalized form is already stored as a Map key at cross-author-utils.ts:139.
architecture_assessment.claim_level_readiness: Nothing in these 1,126 lines can carry a claim record, and the gap is structural rather than a matter of volume. Seven things would have to change. (1) A record type. Today the unit of transfer is a formatted markdown string (corpus-index-provider.ts:126, :143, :156). A claim record needs a stable ID, the claim text, a document ID, a locator (page/Bekker/section), character offsets into the source, a confidence, and links to supporting and contradicting records. None of those survive the current renderers, and `builtAt` — the only provenance field in the whole index — is read by zero code, so there is not even a way to say which build a draft came from. (2) A real retrieval primitive. Substring containment over a lowercased `nodeA + nodeB + description` concatenation (cross-author-utils.ts:525) cannot address a clause. At 70,100 nodes and, say, 2 million claims, an O(n) regex scan per query is not merely slow, it is the wrong shape — this needs the inverted index or the embedding index the project already runs (ChromaDB, gte-Qwen2 at 1536 dims) rather than a hand-rolled scan. Note the ontology already carries `greek`, `transliteration` and `aliases` for 448/170/135 nodes respectively and the matcher consults none of them at the bridge layer, which is why 50 of 72 Greek-source hooks are unreachable from Latin-script topic words. (3) Budgeted selection. Replace fixed record counts with a token budget plus a score threshold, and log emitted-vs-scored. Today the cap silently drops the 55 and reports the 12. (4) Validation at the parse boundary. `JSON.parse` into `any` (jsonl-loaders.ts:198, :211) with zero schema, while the file's own docstring at :6 promises Zod. A ten-line schema requiring non-empty concept fields would have converted six of the CRITICAL findings in this report into startup warnings. (5) Streaming readers. NDJSON via readline instead of readFileSync + split, which also removes the 25x wall and the 150 ms main-thread block that becomes 3.75 s. (6) One cache authority, no derived one-shot flags. Three caches over one file (jsonl-loaders.ts:191, smart-retrieval-layer.ts:795, plus the derivation flag at cross-author-utils.ts:56), keyed on float mtime with no size or hash, handing out live mutable references that one consumer already writes into. (7) No truncation-by-slice. `definition.slice(0, 200)` discards 37.2% of all definition text mid-word; `units.slice(0, 5)` discards 2,259 of 4,059 provenance links. For 'every claim and every clause' the answer is a summarizer or a budget, never a character count.
architecture_assessment.harden_or_replace:
Split the verdict, because the three files are not one thing.

KEEP AND HARDEN the loader/cache layer — jsonl-loaders.ts in full (310 lines) and loadManifestCanonicals (cross-author-utils.ts:77-173). This is genuinely good code. The mtime-cache pattern is right, the Zod boundary for KUs and edges is right (types.ts:93-133 even reports per-record failures with the offending field paths), and the dropped-line counters at :66-68 and :103-105 are exactly the observability the rest of the system lacks. Its defects are mechanical and small: a missing `path` field at :224, a bare catch at :215, a `path`/`size` cache key, and streaming reads. Call it 150 lines of change. The one thing to move INTO this layer is schema validation for compiled-index.json, because the loader is the only chokepoint all three consumers pass through.

REPLACE the matching and rendering layer — getActiveBridges, getActiveTensions, expandQueryWithCanonicalTerms, computeMatchScore, extractTopicWords (cross-author-utils.ts:408-614) and all of corpus-index-provider.ts's scoring and rendering (:79-197). Roughly 600 lines. Hardening these is a trap. Every individual bug has a two-to-six-line fix — guard the empty string at :474, fix `.includes('medium')` at :489, add the `u` flag at corpus-index-provider.ts:179, align the >=4/>=5 thresholds — and you could land all of them in an afternoon and still have a system that carries 0.803% of its index into a prompt as untraceable markdown prose. The bugs are not the problem; the semantics are. Substring containment over lowercased concatenations, absolute record caps, and string-typed output are the architecture, and none of the three survives contact with claim-level records.

Two arguments settle it. First, the empty-string always-match at :474 means the bridge feature has never actually worked on this corpus — there is no working behaviour to preserve, only the appearance of one. Second, `grep -rln` over tests/ finds ZERO tests referencing any of the three modules; the sole check is scripts/verify-hardening.ts, which is in neither CI nor package.json and whose one bridge assertion passes only because its test query contains the literal German word 'Erschlossenheit' that happens to sit in a targetConcept. Nothing depends on current behaviour being stable. That is damning as coverage and liberating as a rewrite constraint — the replacement cost is close to the hardening cost, and only one of the two gets you a system that can hold a claim.

So: foundation in the loaders, obstacle in the matchers. Harden ~450 lines, replace ~600, and write the tests first — every CRITICAL in this report is expressible as a property (an off-topic facet must return zero bridges; no emitted hook may have an empty concept field; derivation must survive a cache invalidation; emitted-vs-scored must be logged) and not one of them is currently asserted anywhere.

result.summary:
I read all 1,126 lines of the three scope files plus ~630 lines of call sites, and verified every claim against the live compiled-index.json, manifest.jsonl, knowledge.jsonl and reasoning.jsonl rather than reasoning from the source alone. All three files are clean vs HEAD, so no dirty-tree line-number skew applies to my scope; the counts match exactly (310/202/614).

The headline is not the cache bug the prior audit flagged. It is that `getActiveBridges` is effectively a constant function. 31 of 72 hooks have `targetConcept: ""`, and cross-author-utils.ts:474 evaluates `t.includes(targetLower)` — which is unconditionally true for an empty string — so those 31 fire for every facet. I simulated the exact code: topic words ['zzzzz','qqqqqq'] return hook-de-anima-07, a record whose targetText, targetConcept, bridge and relevance are all empty. gold-standard-prompt-builder.ts:712-716 then renders it as "**Bridge [hook-de-anima-07]:** Summary Matrix (Aristotle) ↔ ? (Unknown)" followed by "Both authors (Aristotle and Unknown) MUST be cited with direct textual evidence." A mandatory fabrication instruction, on most sections, today.

The `_hooksDerivationDone` claim is confirmed and worse than stated. Grep over src/, tests/ and scripts/ returns exactly the three lines (:56, :342, :351) and no reset. But "no log line" is wrong in a way that matters: icp-orchestrator.ts:364 logs "Bridge activated" and then :368 abandons the backfill silently, so the trace reads as success. And recompile is not the only trigger — `clearJSONLCaches()` clears the index cache without touching the flag, and any caller passing a non-cwd projectRoot thrashes the single-entry path-keyed cache so the fresh parse lands on the second call. When it fires, gold-standard-prompt-builder.ts:712 interpolates with no fallback and the prompt reads "(undefined) ↔ ? (undefined)". TypeScript cannot see this because cross-author-utils.ts:31-33 declares `sourceAuthor: string` as required over data where the key appears zero times.

Two findings the prior audits missed entirely, both in buildCorpusCatalog. It emits a header saying "only suggest from this list" over 117 of the corpus's 578 titles — 635 of 835 ok manifest records have title_raw but no author_raw, so :159-167 never indexes them, which also makes every correct citation of those 461 works fail `isValidAuthorTitlePair`. And :317's `|| 'secondary'` default mislabels 71 of the 117 it does list, including *The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics* and the Greek Kassel and Ross editions, as SECONDARY SCHOLARSHIP.

On the ultimate goal: I measured what actually reaches a prompt. For a well-matched topic it is 5,271 characters out of 656,755 — 0.803% of the index. Six of each ontology node's ten fields are never rendered; tensions ship without their dependencyRelation or conflictRelation; definitions are cut mid-word at 200 chars (37.2% of all definition text unreachable); units are sliced to 5 (2,259 of 4,059 links dropped). The caps are absolute integers, so at 100x volume the emitted context stays the same size and the discard rate goes from ~82% to ~99.8% — the system gets blinder, not slower, and silently. The hard wall arrives earlier than 100x anyway: reasoning.jsonl is 21.5 MB and readFileSync into one JS string throws at Node's 536,870,888-char limit, i.e. ~25x, uncaught at jsonl-loaders.ts:89.

Verdict: the loader/cache layer is a genuine foundation worth ~150 lines of hardening; the ~600-line matching and rendering layer should be replaced, not patched. Every individual bug there has a two-to-six-line fix you could land in an afternoon and still be left carrying 0.8% of the index as untraceable markdown prose — substring containment, fixed caps and string-typed output are the architecture, not the bugs. Two facts make replacement the cheaper option: the bridge feature has never actually worked on this corpus, so there is no behaviour to preserve; and zero test files reference any of these three modules, so nothing depends on it being stable. The only check that exists, scripts/verify-hardening.ts, is in neither CI nor package.json and passes only because its query contains the one German word that happens to sit in a targetConcept.

CONFIRMED. I attempted to refute this on six fronts and every one failed.

1. Line numbers are exact, and both files are CLEAN (`git status --porcelain` on both returns empty), so worktree == HEAD and there is no dirty-tree line drift. faceted-retrieval.ts:154 is `return await this.retrieval.hybridSearch(`, :158 opens the 4th argument object, :164 closes the call; :186/:190/:195 are the second site. smart-retrieval-layer.ts:324-328 declares exactly three parameters (`semanticQuery`, `keywords`, `weights = {semantic:0.7,keyword:0.3}`).

The 4th argument is unreachable at runtime — not merely untyped, but physically dropped.

Nothing type-checks on any run path. `npx tsc --noEmit` emits exactly the two claimed errors, `faceted-retrieval.ts(158,13): error TS2554: Expected 2-3 arguments, but got 4` and `(190,11)` — inside a 157-error total. `package.json:13 "build": "tsc"` and `:23 "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit"` exist but every runtime entry (`observe`, `daemon:start`, `memory:start`, `ucm:*`, `demo`) is `npx tsx` (transpile-only esbuild). 5. The failure scenario IS reachable with shipped code, not hypothetical. icp-api-routes.ts:610 `router.post('/session')` builds a `SourceScopeSpec` at :625-630 with `corpus_config: { collections: [], min_relevance: 0.6, max_chunks: 20 }`, then :633-638 sets `scope.corpus_config.collections = [corpusFolder]` from the request body, and :697-698 constructs `new FacetedRetrieval(factory.deps.retrieval)` and calls `retrieveForAllFacets(promptSpec, scope)` → retrieveForFacet → the per-collection branch at :149. icp-orchestrator.ts:179/:250 is the second live caller. (a) The `collections` field of the discarded argument was doubly dead. `grep -n "collections" smart-retrieval-layer.ts` shows `collections: options.collections || []` normalized once at :194 and read NOWHERE thereafter (all other hits are ChromaDB URL literals). So even with correct arity, collection scoping would still not happen. Saying the facet "got 10 unscoped chunks" is right; implying correct arity would have scoped them is not.

Verified against the live vector store: `vector_db_1536/chroma.sqlite3` contains 57 distinct metadata keys, of which `chunk_id` has 0 rows and `source_id` has 0 rows; the token `source_id` appears nowhere in scripts/ingest/. Both operands are therefore unconditionally undefined and every key degrades to the literal string "undefined:<page_start>". Corpus-wide this collapses 10,731 truly-distinct chunks onto 588 distinct dedup keys; the single key "undefined:1" collides across 83 different authors (Adorno, Ahmed, Aristotle, Bagnoli, Bako, Barnes, ...). Chunks lacking page_start collapse to "undefined:0" because smart-retrieval-layer.ts:980 coerces via `metadata.page_start || 0`. Three minor corrections, none affecting the verdict: (1) the retrieval layer is at src/god-agent/retrieval/smart-retrieval-layer.ts, not src/god-agent/universal/retrieval/ as cited, though the cited line range 972-990 is exact; (2) site pipeline-utils.ts:18 is real but effectively dead — `deduplicateChunks` has no callers beyond the barrel re-export at stages/index.ts:27 — so 19 of the 20 cited sites are live, not 20; (3) site retrieval-stage.ts:303 computes the colliding key only to gate a `c.relevanceScore = 0.85` assignment, with the actual dedup performed by `addChunks` at :311, so :303 manifests as a silently lost relevance boost rather than a dropped chunk — same root cause, slightly different symptom than the reporter framed. Severity CRITICAL is upheld and I failed to argue it down to HIGH: `seenIds` is instantiated once at retrieval-stage.ts:129 and shared across every phase (:227, :344) and exported to the orchestrator (:514, :535, :573), so the collision set accumulates rather than resetting per query. Simulating the real sequence on live data, Phase 1f author-coverage supplementation loses a mean of 2.8 of 8 chunks (36%), which independently confirms the reporter's claim that coverage supplementation "fights a bug it cannot win"; baseline per-draft loss is ~6 of 60 chunks with 99.9% of drafts losing at least one. These numbers use uniform random sampling and therefore UNDERSTATE the real defect, since semantic retrieval clusters on the same works and adjacent page ranges. Bearing on the user's 100x-volume goal: the key's cardinality is bounded by the maximum page number, not by corpus size, so it does not scale at all — at 100x chunk density the same 588 buckets would absorb ~1,073,100 chunks, meaning the defect worsens monotonically as the index grows. Nothing is logged on any drop (retrieval-stage.ts:225-229 and :343-348 are silent; the only recordWarning calls fire on thrown exceptions), and TypeScript cannot flag either access because types.ts:170 declares `[key: string]: any`. The fix is one token: smart-retrieval-layer.ts:973 already assigns `chunkId: ids[i]` to the very object being deduplicated, and Chroma's embedding_id values are unique UUIDs (581,564 distinct), so a correct unique identifier sits one field away from the broken key and is ignored.

CONFIRMED core defect: in the working tree, smart-retrieval-layer.ts:239-241 replaces relevanceScore with the cross-encoder score (assigned at :1262 `relevanceScore: r.relevance_score`), and then :252-290 runs an unconditional +0.10 additive boost with NO guard on `opts.rerank`, re-sorting at :284 before the top-K slice at :293. A lower-reranked chunk that contains a matched canonical substring therefore overtakes a higher-reranked chunk that does not. Term matching at :269 and :277 is `String.includes` — substring, not word-boundary — on both query and chunk content.

CORRECTED SUB-CLAUSE (the one part that is wrong): "both clamp to 1.0 and the top-K slice at :293 becomes arbitrary" is false. `Array.prototype.sort` is stable per ES2019 (verified empirically, 200 elements, order preserved). When two chunks both clamp to 1.0, the comparator returns 0 and the reranker's relative ordering is preserved — the slice degrades to the pre-boost order, it does not randomize. The real harm from clamping is different and still real: it collapses score MARGINS (0.97 and 0.93 both become 1.0), corrupting relevanceScore as a confidence signal for downstream consumers such as section-orchestrator.ts:588-590, which sums `chunk.relevanceScore` to compute an average-relevance metric.

AGGRAVATING FACTOR 1 (worse than reported) — blast radius. smart-retrieval-layer.ts:924-927 widens the candidate pool to `Math.min(maxChunks * rerankCandidateMultiplier(), 50)` (multiplier defaults to 3 at :1206) whenever rerank is active. The boost re-sorts that entire pool of up to 50 chunks before :293 slices to maxChunks. A chunk sitting at reranked rank 50 can be promoted into the final top-10 — the reporter's example understates this as an A/B swap.

AGGRAVATING FACTOR 2 (worse than reported) — the collision surface is not an edge case. `Ding` is a canonical term (length 4, passes the :269 guard) and is a substring of "understanding", "reading", "according", "regarding", "including". I attempted to refute this claim on six fronts and it survived five of them; only one sub-clause broke.

1. Line-number drift (the strongest refutation candidate given the dirty-worktree warning). FAILED to refute. `git status --porcelain` reports smart-retrieval-layer.ts as clean, so worktree == HEAD for this file. I read every cited line and each matches verbatim: :239-241, :268-270, :273-284, :1262. No off-by-one.

2. Unreachable code / rerank never actually enabled. FAILED to refute. `rerank` defaults to false at :201, which initially looked promising — but two production call sites pass `rerank: true` explicitly (pdf-analysis-pipeline.ts:384, section-orchestrator.ts:584), and the master switch `isRerankEnabled()` at :1186-1191 returns true by default, reinforced by config-manager.ts:286 `enabled: true`. Both paths land in `retrieveContext`, so the boost runs immediately downstream of a real cross-encoder score.

3. A guard elsewhere that suppresses the boost when reranking is on. FAILED to refute. The Step 4c block never reads `opts.rerank`; :256 unconditionally seeds `termBoosted = kgBoosted`. Worse for the code's defence, the `rerankResults` docstring at :1213-1214 states the boosts are *designed* to stack on the cross-encoder — so this is intended behaviour, which makes it a design defect rather than an oversight, not a non-defect.

4. The boost is silently dead (swallowed by the bare `catch { }` at :290). FAILED to refute, and this is the most interesting finding. The comment at :262-264 documents that the boost WAS previously dead — it referenced `enrichedQuery`, which is scoped to `semanticSearch()`, throwing a ReferenceError that :290 swallowed. That bug has been fixed to use the in-scope `query` parameter. So the boost is newly live; the defect is active, not historical.

5. Scenario unreachable with real repo data. FAILED to refute. I reproduced the reporter's "measured" term set exactly against the real compiled-index.json: `["Incorporation","rhetoric","Rhetoric","Rede"]`, confirming 'Rede' matches inside "Redemption". All 1,722/1,709 counts check out, and all 18 named generic terms are present.

6. Consequence overstated. PARTIALLY succeeded — this is the one place the reporter is wrong. The clause "both clamp to 1.0 and the top-K slice at :293 becomes arbitrary" is false, because `Array.prototype.sort` has been stable since ES2019 (I verified empirically with 200 tied elements). Tied entries retain the reranker's ordering, so the slice degrades to the pre-boost order rather than randomizing. The genuine clamping harm is margin destruction, not order randomization — and it does have a real downstream consumer, since section-orchestrator.ts:588-590 averages `relevanceScore` as a quality metric that clamping inflates toward 1.0.

Against that one correction, I found two aggravating factors the reporter missed, both of which push severity up rather than down. First, :924-927 widens the reranked candidate pool to min(maxChunks*3, 50) precisely when rerank is active, and the boost re-sorts that whole pool before :293 slices — so promotion is not a neighbourly A/B swap, it can lift a rank-50 chunk into the final top-10. Second, the substring collision is systemic rather than incidental: 'Ding' is a length-4 canonical term that passes the :269 guard and is a substring of "understanding", "reading", "according", "regarding", and "including". It fired on all three realistic dissertation queries I tested, meaning the boost injects noise on essentially every query the system will ever see.

Judged against the user's stated goal of a claim-and-clause-level index, this is exactly the wrong direction: the boost is a bag-of-substrings heuristic layered on top of, and overriding, the one measured semantic improvement in the stack. The project's own eval verdict recorded that the reranker is the win; I searched for any eval artifact validating this +0.10 heuristic and found none.

Verdict: not refuted. HIGH is the correct severity — the corrected sub-clause is cosmetic relative to the confirmed mechanism, and the two aggravating factors more than offset it.

I defaulted to refuted=true and worked through every listed failure mode; none applies.

LINE NUMBERS — not a HEAD/worktree artifact. `git status --porcelain` on retrieval-utils.ts, retrieval-stage.ts, and gold-standard-config.ts returns EMPTY: all three are clean, so HEAD and working tree are identical here and the dirty-tree caveat is moot. Seven further call sites exist in the orchestrator. Not dead code.

GUARD / NARROWING ELSEWHERE — none. I looked for (a) an elision marker: absent, the join is a bare `' '`; (b) a pristine pre-trim copy: absent, `chunk.content = trimChunkContent(chunk.content, ...)` mutates the shared ContextChunk objects, so `allChunks` and every downstream holder see the collage; (c) a re-fetch of original text in the validator: absent, findTextInCorpusChunks (:480-496) and findBestTextMatch (:512-525) read only `this.corpusChunks[].content`; (d) prompt-side framing that would warn the model: the nearest thing is write-pipeline-orchestrator.ts:750, which warns only that chunks are "raw OCR output" with "formatting artifacts" and then instructs "When directly quoting, extract ONLY the meaningful scholarly text" — that hedge does not disclose sentence removal and actively invites verbatim extraction from the collage, so it aggravates rather than mitigates.

SILENT-FAILURE-THAT-ACTUALLY-LOGS — I checked this specifically because it is the most common refutation. The orchestrator copy does log (`Phase 1d: Chunk trimming: X → Y avg chars/chunk`, write-pipeline-orchestrator.ts:1968), but the newer staged path at retrieval-stage.ts:318-320 has no logging whatsoever. So the migration to stages made it strictly quieter. Either way the log reports only a char-count delta and would never reveal non-contiguity.

SCENARIO REACHABLE WITH REAL DATA — yes, demonstrated. Running the exact algorithm (transcribed line-for-line, with the real conceptPattern built from the 46 keyConcepts in .god-agent/domain-config.json via buildConceptPattern at domain-config.ts:133-136) over real corpus/index Heidegger prose: 3 of 3 sampled 2,000-char windows produced non-contiguous collages, including sentences [0,4,9] out of 12 — structurally identical to the reporter's hypothesized S2/S7/S11. CONSEQUENCE OVERSTATED? — No. The claim that no downstream validator can catch it is mechanically true because the trim is an in-place mutation and the validator's ground truth is the same object. A quote spanning a seam is an exact substring of `chunk.content`, so extractMostSimilarSubstring returns it at similarity 1.0 and classifyMatch (:247-252) returns 'verbatim'. Combined with the page attribution stamped at gold-standard-prompt-builder.ts:149, a fabricated sentence is emitted with a confident, validator-blessed page cite.

Only nuance worth flagging, and it does not reduce severity: the collage is a *sentence-level* recombination, so each individual sentence remains verbatim; fabrication requires the model to quote ACROSS a seam. Given the prompt explicitly directs direct quotation from these blocks and 450 chars typically holds only 2-3 sentences with the seams invisible, that is a routine outcome, not an exotic one. CRITICAL stands, and is reinforced by the project's own standing instruction that citation rigor is UTMOST PRIORITY.

result.reasoning:
The quoted code is real and the line numbers are exact against the dirty working tree, so this is not a citation failure. The claim collapses on four independent grounds.

1. The counting is true but materially misleading. 153 of 190 pipe rows do lie outside the window, but 91 of those 153 belong to tables that must never become ontology nodes: Rickert's `## 3B: Global Edge List` (58 rows of edge records), Uexkull's `## 3C. Productive Tensions` (11), and Burke's `## (ix) Tier distribution` (22 rows of a Tier|Count|Description summary with only 3 data rows). The restriction is deliberate and documented — the sibling parser states the rationale outright at :221-222.

2. The proposed defect inverts cause and effect. I simulated the fix in memory: feeding Rickert's whole file to the same row loop yields 62 fabricated nodes named `depends_on`, `presupposes`, `contrasts_with`, each carrying edge-rationale prose in centralityTier. The window is what stops the index from being poisoned. This is the opposite of silent data loss.

3. The headline scenario is factually wrong. The report asserts "the function returns [] and both tables are lost." The 33/36-row canonical node table is not lost: parse_header_ontology has a second, independent path at :533-536 that splits on `#### N.` headers across the whole document, and it harvests the hand-mirrored `## 3A. Canonical Node List` at :149 — a section whose own text says it is "harvested by scripts/compile-corpus-index.py." All 36 rows resolve in compiled-index.json, 0 missing. HR ships 30 nodes. The reporter traced only the table path and never checked whether the concepts arrived by another route.

4. Both stated consequences misattribute their cause. The Contributors column is genuinely absent, but not because of the window: `_parse_uexkull_table_row` at :627-674 has no contributors branch and hardcodes `"aliases": []`, and the emitted node schema has no such field. Widening the window would not recover it — it would corrupt: HR's header `| # | Canonical Name | German | Greek | Contributors | Aliases |` hits positional fallbacks, giving type=Greek (pos 3), centralityTier="all 8" (pos 4, the Contributors cell), definition=alias text (pos 5). Likewise the 30 concordance links are genuinely missing, but `_parse_header_tables` produces ontologyNodes and structurally cannot produce a hook; the sole cause is the Aristotle-only glob at :1239-1244. The closing inference — "this is one reason no non-Aristotle text has any [hook]" — is therefore false; that hardcoded path is the entire reason.

One further precision error: for all four files the `^##\s+3A[.:]` regex actually DOES match. The empty return comes from the `if "|" not in section_text` check at :569-570, not the `if not m` branch at :559-560 the report emphasizes.

What genuinely survives is small: an unlogged empty return (no warn() at either exit) and roughly 19 rows of never-ingested content in Uexkull 3C and Rickert 3D, of which exactly one concept name ("Attunement") is missing from the index. That is a LOW coverage gap, not a HIGH silent-data-loss defect.

Against the user's stated goal — claim- and clause-level records at ~100x volume — this episode is diagnostic in a way the report misses. The real obstacle is not the window but the fixed 10-key node schema and a positional table reader that silently mis-slots any column it does not recognize. Rickert's 58 edge rows, Uexkull's 11 tensions, and HR's 30 concordance links are exactly the "points of connection" the goal names, and the architecture has nowhere to put them: one flat ontologyNodes array with no relation, contributor, or provenance-span slot. Widening regexes cannot fix that; it needs a typed multi-record emitter (node / edge / tension / hook / claim) with header-name-driven rather than positional column binding.

The reporter quoted the code accurately — :167-171 are verbatim correct and the file is clean, so there is no line-number drift. The data figures (531 phase-less, 518 under corpus/index/) also reproduce exactly. What fails is the causal story built on top of those true observations.

1. Phase 1 has no vectors to give. run_ingest.py:13 states "NO embeddings" and :352 repeats it in the CLI help. The scenario says a record is "never superseded" and thus never upgraded — but supersession by run_ingest.py would append another record built from record_base (:395-408), which contains no `phase` key and follows no embedding call. Even with the skip disabled entirely, the record would remain phase-less and vector-less. The skip predicate is therefore not the mechanism that produces or preserves the no-vector state; it is orthogonal to it. The consequence ("a permanently stuck no-vector state that no re-run of the Phase-1 tool can clear") is technically true only in the vacuous sense that a tool which never writes vectors cannot clear a no-vector state — that is not a defect in the skip predicate.

2. The state is demonstrably not stuck. should_skip_phase2 (:312-330) is phase-aware exactly as the reporter notes, and that is precisely why the 531 records are rescued rather than trapped: `phase_ok = int(rec.get("phase") or 0) >= 2` evaluates False for every one of them, so :325-326 returns False and all 531 are processed. I replayed the real predicate over the real manifest: 0 skipped, 531 processed. "Permanently self-perpetuating" is refuted by the repo's own data.

3. Phase 2 does not consume Phase 1's skip decisions. The reporter's scenario implicitly treats the manifest as a work queue Phase 1 gatekeeps. It is not. run_ingest_phase2.py:982 does its own `root.rglob("*")` over the filesystem and consults the manifest only as a per-file skip lookup at :1141. A Phase-1 `continue` at :420 cannot remove a file from Phase 2's candidate set. The two tools are coupled only through a record store, not a queue.

4. An explicit escape hatch exists and went unmentioned: `--force` at :842, gated in at :1141 as `(not args.force) and should_skip_phase2(...)`, bypasses skip logic outright. "No re-run can clear" is false even setting aside points 1-3.

The watch_corpus.py:155-157 early-return on Phase 2 failure is real code, but it does not create permanence: it is a transient per-event abort that logs at :156 (the reporter concedes the log, which also defeats the "silent" framing), and the next Phase 2 run re-walks the entire root and re-processes every phase-less record anyway.

Because run_ingest.py never writes `phase`, importing phase2's predicate into should_skip would create a condition that can never be satisfied, so every Phase-1 invocation would re-chunk and re-append all 531 records indefinitely, growing manifest.jsonl without bound and worsening the very latest-record-wins duplication (1,182 lines → 696 unique paths) already present. The existing predicate — content unchanged AND last attempt succeeded — is the correct skip semantics for a structure-only planner.

The provider is constructed unconditionally at icp-provider-factory.ts:95, and prompt-decomposer.ts:106-108 takes the LLM path whenever `this.llm` is set. I confirmed reachability empirically by executing the real exported function.

4. Overstated consequence. This was the one place the reporter needed correcting, and it cuts both ways. Understated: the reporter treated this as a labelling cosmetic, but DECOMPOSITION_SYSTEM_PROMPT:44 explicitly instructs the model to *trust* the categorization ("pre-categorized into PRIMARY TEXTS (the authors' own works) and SECONDARY SCHOLARSHIP (commentary)"), and the suggestions propagate through icp-orchestrator.ts:229-241 into sourcePriority.secondarySources and then into llm-claim-provider.ts:220's "=== SECONDARY SOURCE EVIDENCE (use for interpretation and commentary) ===" block, which caps at 20 spans versus 40 for primary. Overstated: that propagation needs `sourcePriority` truthy (icp-orchestrator.ts:215), and llm-claim-provider.ts:191 checks user-declared primaryPatterns first, so an explicitly declared primary source still routes correctly at span-grouping; also "mislabelling 71 of 117" overcounts, since the Aristotle commentators and most of the RDR2/VR cluster among those 71 are genuinely secondary and land correctly by accident.

The single strongest piece of evidence is one the reporter did not find: the rendered catalog contradicts itself within the same list. "Aristotle: Rhetoric" sits under PRIMARY TEXTS while "Aristotle: Ars Rhetorica (Greek, Rudolf Kassel)" sits under SECONDARY SCHOLARSHIP — same for Physics/Physica, On The Soul/De Anima (Ross_Greek), and Being and Time vs GA 29/30. That is a stronger false signal than a uniform default would be: it tells the model the Greek critical editions are commentary *on* the English translations, inverting the actual scholarly relation.

I settled on HIGH rather than CRITICAL. The mechanism is confirmed and it silently degrades the primary/secondary distinction on every ICP run, which bears directly on the citation rigor the user flags as utmost priority. But it corrupts prompt framing and source *suggestion*, not retrieval (which keys on facet descriptions and terms, never on tier), and it neither fabricates citations nor corrupts verbatim text; a user-supplied sourcePriority partially compensates downstream. "The model will hedge or mis-frame citations" is a plausible but unproven behavioral inference, and the 61% figure describes unverified defaults rather than confirmed mislabels.

On the programme's larger question: this is the same architectural pathology seen across the compiler — a falsy-default that silently substitutes a plausible wrong value for missing data, with no counter, no warning, and no way to distinguish "known secondary" from "never classified". At claim-level and clause-level volumes (~100x), a 61% unverified-default rate becomes unauditable. The minimal fix is a third state: emit 'UNCLASSIFIED WORKS (tier not yet assigned — do not assume commentary)' as its own catalog section and log the count, rather than laundering absence into a positive assertion.

## 7. Scalability ceiling — the section that decides the programme

**Target:** claim-level and clause-level records for every document. Sizing from the actual corpus: 224 ingested documents × ~200 claims ≈ **45,000 claim records**; × ~10 clauses ≈ **450,000 clause records**. At the stated 100x that is ~4.5M claims / ~45M clauses. At the measured 712 bytes/record that is **~32 MB** at claim level today and **~320 MB** at clause level; at 100x, ~22 GB.

### Component-by-component breaking points

| Component | Breaks at | Why — with the number |
|---|---|---|
| **Compiler** (`compile-corpus-index.py`) | **Already broken. 1x.** | Runtime is not the constraint (48 files, <1 s; 100x is still seconds). What breaks is **silence**: 0 warnings while discarding 37.6% of header source, 70.2% of hook prose, 55 of 119 tensions, 70 nodes. At 100x that is ~200 silently corrupt nodes and ~18 MB of silently discarded source, with exit 0 every time. **Registration** is a 19-key hand-maintained literal that has already lost 8 of 27 directories; at 100x it needs ~1,900 hand-written entries. And the emitted schema has **no slot for provenance** — the parsers work on `text.splitlines()` and `re.split()` and discard offsets in the first statement of every function (`:244`, `:326`, `:533`, `:577`, `:679`, `:701`), so there is no point in the code where a byte offset is still available. |
| **Artifact format** (single pretty-printed JSON) | **~30–50 MB, i.e. ~50x.** | 664,494 B for 701 nodes = 712 B/record; `indent=2` alone costs 137,323 B (20.7%). Node parses it in 3.8 ms for **5.7 MB heap — 8.6× expansion** — and does so twice per process. 320 MB of clause-level JSON ⇒ ~2.8 GB heap per parse, ~1.8 s of blocked event loop, twice. V8's `MAX_STRING_LENGTH` (536,870,888) is a hard wall on `readFileSync('utf-8')` regardless of RAM. And it is **git-tracked and rewritten in full on every build**, with `builtAt` + 202 hash-ordered positions guaranteeing a diff even for a no-op — a 32 MB churning tracked file makes the repository unreviewable. |
| **Loader** (`jsonl-loaders.ts:89`, `:210`) | **24.97x — not 100x.** | `reasoning.jsonl` is 21,498,945 B today. `readFileSync` into one JS string throws `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG` at 536,870,888 chars. Two different undiagnosable failures from one cause: `:89` throws **uncaught** (process death); `:210` is inside the bare catch → **silent total blackout**. `raw.split('\n')` doubles peak memory and blocks the event loop 150 ms today → 3.75 s at 25x, synchronously, inside daemons. |
| **Cache layer** | **Already degrading at 1x; no ceiling because it never grows.** | 30-min TTL LRU, 1,000 entries, **O(n) eviction per insert at capacity**, each entry up to 28 chunk bodies (~84 MB at 3 KB/chunk). **Nothing invalidates on re-ingest.** The mutation-through-cache defect means it caches derivatives, not the corpus. `_hooksDerivationDone` and `protectedTerms` never invalidate at all. At claim level, cache entries become claim sets and the entry-count cap becomes meaningless. |
| **Retrieval path** | **Pool cap 50 — a hard constant, at any volume.** | `smart-retrieval-layer.ts:926` caps the candidate pool at `Math.min(maxChunks*3, 50)`; no configuration exceeds it (perversely, rerank OFF gives `maxChunks*2` = up to 80, so enabling the reranker *narrows* the pool). The KG boost is a pure linear scan: today `5,437 + |topicConcepts|×5,437 + |expansionConcepts|×5,437` ≈ **1.2M iterations per sub-query**, ×8–15 sub-queries. At 100x (58,800 KUs, 543,700 edges) that is **~120M iterations per sub-query** — tens of seconds of single-threaded JS each — with both arrays fully resident. Canonical-boost is O(1,722) substring tests per query → ~170,000 at 100x. The `undefined:page_start` de-dup key **gets worse with volume** because more works share low page numbers. |
| **Prompt builder** | **Two opposite walls.** | `corpus-index-provider.ts:101-103` caps are **absolute integers**, so at 100x the emitted context is byte-identical while the discard rate goes **82% → 99.8%** — the system does not get slower, it gets proportionally blinder, silently. Conversely `buildCorpusCatalog` (`cross-author-utils.ts:307-331`) is the **one** component that scales linearly: 8,439 chars / ~2,110 tokens today → **~844 KB / ~211,000 tokens at 100x**, injected uncapped into every decomposition prompt. Hard wall at **~90x**, with quality degradation well before. |
| **Reasoner** (`reason_over_knowledge.py`) | **Already at 86% of budget.** | 588 KUs → 25,334 intra + 147,244 cross = **172,578 pairs against a 200,000 default**. One more corpus entry and the cross-author pass at `:349` silently never runs — it only `break`s. At 100x, 1.73 billion pairs. `char_ngrams` recomputed inside the inner loop: 345,156 calls for 588 distinct claims. Anchoring is ~289 s today → **~80 h at 100x**, single-threaded, with no incremental mode. |

And because `SKIP_DIRS` lacks `"index"` and 518/522 index records carry a falsy `phase`, **all 516 index markdown files are re-chunked and re-embedded on every compile** — the index gets more expensive to ingest the more index there is. |

### Recommendation: **REPLACE the parse-and-emit layer. HARDEN the loaders, the orchestration, and the reasoner's skeleton.**

I am not hedging: the split is the answer, and each half is argued below.

**REPLACE — `compile-corpus-index.py`'s parse and emit layers (~1,100 of 1,412 lines), `normalize-edges.py` (306 lines, entire), `merge-reasoning-edges.py` (237 lines, entire), and the TS matching/rendering layer (`cross-author-utils.ts:408-614` + `corpus-index-provider.ts:79-197`, ~600 lines).**

Four pieces of evidence, in order of force.

1. **The structured data already exists and the compiler ignores it.** `grep -c "ontology.json"` over 1,412 lines returns **0**, while **12 `*-ontology.json` files sit in the same directories the compiler scrapes**. *Heidegger and Rhetoric*'s is 56,912 bytes with structured `canonical_nodes` carrying `contributors` and `cross_pipeline_links`, `contested_concepts` with per-contributor readings, and a `tension_summary` — precisely the fields the markdown scrape loses. **The pipeline is doing the hardest possible job — recovering structure from prose — when the structure is on disk in the same folder.** Hardening a scraper that competes with a structured twin is work spent to reach a worse result. This single fact decides the harden-or-replace question.

2. **The defect density is architectural, not incidental.** In one 500-line window: 2 corrupt shipped nodes, 17+ silent-discard branches, 4 dead/unreachable blocks, 3 latent silent-row-deletion paths, zero tests. The bugs are not independent — they descend from one decision, to parse a structured document with line-at-a-time regex and mutable flags. The *same* unbounded-section bug exists independently in **two** parsers (`:308` and `:718`), which is what happens when three markdown dialects get three hand-rolled scanners instead of one grammar. Fixing `:718` fixes 2 nodes; it does not make `:539-540`, `:558`, `:606`, `:611-614` or the absent provenance any less true.

3. **The schema is a dead end for the stated goal, and that is not tunable.** A claim record is `(text, source_path, heading_path, line_start, line_end, char_start, char_end, type, subject, polarity, evidence_refs)`. The emitted dict has ten flat fields and **not one is an identity or an anchor**. Adding provenance is not a schema addition — it requires the parsers to track offsets, which none of them do, at any point. Meanwhile the corpus already *contains* claim-level records: `metaphysics-ontology.md` `## 3. Key Positions` is 14 numbered claims each with a Bekker locus and a status, and this code absorbs all fourteen into the ὄρεξις node's `fields` dict as keys `'1'..'14'` and drops them at `:379-390`. **The data exists; the schema has nowhere to put it.** Likewise the compiler demonstrably parses Rickert's tension structure (`node a`, `node b`, `dependency edge`, `conflict edge`, `synthesis`) and then throws 732 bytes away in the same function call, because the return dict has no slot.

4. **Nothing depends on current behaviour, so the replacement cost ≈ the hardening cost.** `grep -rln` over `tests/` finds **zero** tests referencing any of the three TS modules; the sole check is `scripts/verify-hardening.ts`, in neither CI nor `package.json`, whose one bridge assertion passes only because its query happens to contain a literal German word sitting in a `targetConcept`. And the always-true `t.includes('')` at `cross-author-utils.ts:474` means **the bridge feature has never actually worked on this corpus** — there is no working behaviour to preserve, only the appearance of one.

**HARDEN — `jsonl-loaders.ts` (310 lines), `loadManifestCanonicals` (`cross-author-utils.ts:77-173`), `god_learn.py`'s orchestration, `reason_over_knowledge.py`'s pair machinery, and `compile-corpus-index.py:195-1025` as adapters.**

This code is genuinely good and rewriting it would be pure risk. The mtime-cache pattern is right; the Zod boundary for KUs and edges is right (`types.ts:93-134` even reports per-record failures with offending field paths); the dropped-line counters at `jsonl-loaders.ts:66-68` and `:103-105` are exactly the observability the rest of the system lacks. The HTTP wiring to the embedding API and Chroma (`smart-retrieval-layer.ts:898-945`) is correct, the `kind: 'query'` asymmetry fix at `:901` was hard-won, and the rerank integration (`:1220-1286`) is well-structured with an AbortController timeout, index validation, and preserved `retrievalScore`. The five parsers at `:195-1025` handle four genuinely different markdown dialects that real analysts produced over a year and they *work* (771 nodes, zero exceptions) — even the one that fails (RDR2 Secondary's `- **Name** — gloss — units · Tier` bullets → 0 nodes) fails by omission, not corruption. **Lift them out as per-format adapters; do not rewrite them.**

**The smallest replacement that preserves the authored content.** The corpus under `corpus/index` — 30.9 MB, 1,848 files, 240 CSVs, 22 manifests, 12 structured ontology JSONs — is the real asset and must not be touched. Concretely:

1. **Invert the source of truth.** Read `*-ontology.json` where present; treat markdown as rendering. Make a missing JSON an *error*, not a silent fallback. This immediately recovers `contributors`, `cross_pipeline_links`, `contested_concepts` and `tension_summary` that the scrape currently loses.
2. **Lift `:195-1025` out as adapters** (they are already nearly pure functions of `(text, label)`), giving each an offset cursor and an `extra` passthrough for unrecognised keys.
3. **Rewrite `:1181-1412`** (~250 lines) as a schema-first loader: discover entries from `_synthesis/manifest.json` (22 exist), validate every record, assign stable ids with `(source_path, heading_path, line span, char span)`, refuse to publish on zero-node parses or unexplained count drops, and exit non-zero.
4. **Shard the artifact per entry** with a manifest; move to SQLite/FTS5 (the repo's existing idiom) for anything claim-level, with an inverted term→claim index and a concept→edge adjacency map so boosting becomes O(terms in chunk) rather than O(total claims).
5. **Add a CSV adapter** so the 240 files / 20,610 curated edge rows — the densest, most locus-bearing content in the index, currently at 0% runtime reachability — become first-class records.

Estimate: **2–4 weeks**, and it *deletes* more of `compile-corpus-index.py` than it ports. Against that, hardening the CRITICAL/HIGH list alone is ~15 structural items requiring provenance threading through five parsers, a markdown AST to replace `:244-289`/`:335-344`/`:701-724`, a claim/clause record model, and a validation harness — a **larger** diff that arrives without the provenance the current design has no slot for.

**One decisive piece of context.** The docstring at `:14-15` has promised stderr warnings since the file was written, and the mechanism emits **nothing at all** on the live corpus. The design has been failing silently for its entire history with zero observability, and every number in this report had to be recovered by re-running the parsers by hand. That is not a system to tune. **Verdict: the markdown/JSON corpus under `corpus/index` is an excellent foundation. `scripts/compile-corpus-index.py`'s parse-and-emit layer and the TS matching layer are obstacles and should be replaced.**
